contentMarkdown:
An audio cutter online free is the fastest way to trim an MP3, cut a clip out of a long recording, or make a ringtone — no software to install, no account to create, and no file to upload to a stranger's server. Open the cutter in your browser, drop in your audio file, mark where the clip starts and ends, and download the trimmed piece as an MP3. This guide walks through the exact steps, the formats that work, and the honest limits worth knowing before you cut.

![Audio mixer and headphones on a desk, trimming an audio clip with an online audio cutter](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1470225620780-dba8ba36b745?w=1200&q=80)

## How to cut audio online free

The whole job takes under a minute once your file is loaded. Cutting happens entirely in your browser with an audio engine that runs locally on your device, so your recording is never uploaded, stored, or seen by anyone.

### Step 1: Open the free audio cutter and upload your file

Open the [free Audio Cutter tool](/tools/audio-cutter) and drop in your audio file, or click to browse your files. It accepts MP3, WAV, M4A, FLAC, OGG, Opus, and AAC files up to about 100 MB — a podcast episode, a voice memo, a song, or a lecture recording all work. The file loads and you can play it back right in the page to find the part you want.

### Step 2: Find your cut points

Listen through the audio and note where your clip should start and end. You can type the start and end times in seconds directly, or pause playback at the exact moment and press "Use current ▶ start/end" to set a cut point at the playback position. Take a moment here — a cut that starts a fraction of a second early sounds much better than one that chops off the first word or the first beat.

### Step 3: Export the trimmed clip as MP3

Press "Cut & export MP3", preview the result, and download your clip. The output is always an MP3 at 192 kbps, which plays on every phone, browser, and audio editor. If the preview sounds wrong — the cut starts too late, or you kept too much silence at the end — just adjust the times and export again. Nothing is locked in until you download.

## What audio formats can you cut?

Most audio you have lying around will work. The cutter accepts MP3, WAV, M4A, FLAC, OGG, Opus, and AAC, up to roughly 100 MB per file. Whatever goes in, the trimmed clip always comes out as an MP3 at 192 kbps — a deliberate choice, because MP3 plays everywhere: phones, messaging apps, video editors, and ringtone settings.

The one trade-off is re-encoding: your clip is converted to MP3 at 192 kbps even if the original was a lossless WAV or FLAC. For normal listening — ringtones, voice clips, podcast highlights, social media audio — the difference is inaudible. If you are archiving a master recording, keep the original file untouched and treat the MP3 as the working copy.

## Cut an MP3 into a ringtone

This is the most common reason people search for an MP3 cutter, and it takes about thirty seconds. Pick the catchiest 15–30 seconds of a song — usually the chorus or the hook — and trim everything else away. A ringtone longer than 30 seconds gets cut off by most phones anyway, so shorter is better.

On Android, the exported MP3 can usually be set as a ringtone directly from your sound settings. On iPhone, ringtones need the M4R format, so the MP3 needs one extra step in GarageBand or a converter before it can be set — the cutter gives you a clean MP3 starting point, but it does not produce M4R files itself. Either way, trim the clip first, then worry about the format.

## Free online audio cutter vs desktop apps

Desktop editors like Audacity are free and far more powerful: multi-track editing, fades, noise reduction, and effects. If you edit audio every week, learning one is worth it. But for a single quick cut, the browser wins on every practical measure — no install, no learning curve, no project files to manage, and your audio never leaves your device.

| Option | Best for | Install? | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Browser audio cutter | One quick trim, ringtones, clips | No | Free |
| Audacity | Regular editing, fades, effects | Yes — free | Free |
| Phone audio apps | Cutting on the go | Yes — varies | Often paid or ad-supported |

If the job is "cut this one clip right now," the online cutter is the right tool. If the job is "produce a podcast episode," open a real editor.

## Tips for a clean cut

A few habits make the difference between a clip that sounds professional and one that sounds chopped:

- **Cut on silence or a beat.** Starting a clip mid-word or mid-note is the most common mistake. Zoom in on the quiet gap before the sound you want.
- **Leave a breath of room.** A tenth of a second of silence at the start sounds natural; cutting exactly on the first sound feels abrupt.
- **Listen to the preview.** The cutter lets you hear the result before downloading — use it. Re-exporting costs seconds; re-cutting after you have shared the file costs much more.
- **Keep the original.** Always keep the full recording. You can re-cut from it any time, but you can never restore audio you trimmed away.

## Limits to know before you cut

An honest tool page should say what it cannot do. The file cap is about 100 MB, so a very long uncompressed WAV may need compressing first — an MP3 of the same recording will be far smaller. Each run handles one file, so a batch of clips means repeating the three steps per file. And because the cutting engine loads in your browser the first time you open the tool, you need an internet connection to get started, even though the audio itself never uploads.

None of these limits matter for the usual jobs — trimming a voice memo, cutting a song into a ringtone, pulling a quote out of an interview. They only matter if you are processing hours of audio or building a library of clips, in which case a desktop editor is the better fit.
